clinical_knowledge.topic: Breast Cancer (suspicious mass, pending biopsy) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Breast Cancer (suspicious mass, pending biopsy) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Breast Cancer: Order mammogram and ultrasound, refer for core needle biopsy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Breast Cancer (suspicious mass, pending biopsy).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Fibroadenoma (benign, mobile) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy — suggests more advanced disease.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A painless, firm lump in the breast — especially in the upper outer quadrant, where most breast cancers arise — that requires imaging and biopsy to confirm malignancy.
red_flags: Skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy — suggests more advanced disease

must_ask.say: When did you first notice the lump?
Is it firm, and does it move when you press on it?
Any dimpling, puckering, or nipple changes?
Have you felt anything in your armpit?
Does breast cancer run in your family?
